A finite rooted directed tree $T=(V,E)$ has root $o$, with all edges directed away from $o$, and a nonempty receiver set $R$ consisting of every leaf other than $o$. Every nonroot internal vertex has at least two children. For a vertex $v$, its children are the vertices joined to $v$ by an outgoing edge; $P(o,v)$ is the unique edge set on the path from $o$ to $v$. The root may have any finite number of children.

A finite probe design is a nonempty finite family $\mathcal C=((C_d,N_d))_{d=1}^D$, where each receiver set $C_d$ is a nonempty subset of $R$ and each probe count $N_d$ is a positive integer. A singleton receiver set is a unicast scheme; a receiver set of size at least two is a multicast scheme. Its used edge set is $E_d=\bigcup_{r\in C_d}P(o,r)$.

For a link-success parameter vector $p=(p_e)_{e\in E}\in(0,1)^E$, each design $d$ and probe $j\in\{1,\ldots,N_d\}$ has mutually independent link-success variables $X_{e,d,j}\in\{0,1\}$ for $e\in E_d$, with $\Pr_p(X_{e,d,j}=1)=p_e$. The same $p_e$ applies in every design and probe (temporal homogeneity). The observed receiver indicator is
$$
Y_{r,d,j}=\prod_{e\in P(o,r)}X_{e,d,j}\qquad(r\in C_d).
$$

For $y\in\{0,1\}^{C_d}$ let
$$
\Omega_{d,y}=\left\{x\in\{0,1\}^{E_d}: y_r=\prod_{e\in P(o,r)}x_e\text{ for every }r\in C_d\right\},\qquad w_{p,d}(x)=\prod_{e\in E_d}p_e^{x_e}(1-p_e)^{1-x_e}.
$$
The one-probe outcome law is
$$
P_{p,d}(y)=\sum_{x\in\Omega_{d,y}}w_{p,d}(x).
$$
These probabilities sum to one because the sets $\Omega_{d,y}$ partition the finite link-state space and $\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{E_d}}w_{p,d}(x)=\prod_{e\in E_d}(p_e+(1-p_e))=1$. The complete experiment observes $N_d$ independent outcomes with law $P_{p,d}$ for each design, independently across designs. If the data are summarized by counts, $n_{d,y}\in\mathbb N_0$ is the number of probes in design $d$ with outcome $y$, and $\sum_y n_{d,y}=N_d$.

This is a finite statistical experiment: its parameter space is $(0,1)^E$ and its sampling law is the finite product of the stated receiver-outcome laws.

For a finite-tree probe design $\mathcal C=((C_d,N_d))_{d=1}^D$, a receiver $r\in R$ is **covered** if $r\in C_d$ for some $d$. For a nonroot internal vertex $v$, a design $C_d$ **splits** $v$ if there are distinct children $c,c'$ of $v$ and receivers $r,s\in C_d$ such that $r$ lies in the subtree rooted at $c$ and $s$ lies in the subtree rooted at $c'$. The design satisfies the **split/coverage condition** if every receiver is covered and every nonroot internal vertex is split by at least one design.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

derivations.claim: For each vertex $v$, put $q_v=\prod_{e\in P(o,v)}p_e$, with $q_o=1$. Because $N_d\ge1$, the repeated-probe law for design $d$ has one-probe marginal $P_{p,d}$; conversely, equality of all one-probe laws gives equality of $\mathsf L(p)$. For each covered leaf $r$, the marginal success probability read from any design containing $r$ is $m_r=\Pr_p(Y_r=1)=q_r$. Thus equality of experiment laws determines every $q_r$ when all receivers are covered.

If a receiver $r$ is uncovered, its terminal edge $e=(u,r)$ occurs in no observed path. Changing $p_e$ to a different value in $(0,1)$ leaves every observed outcome law unchanged, because $r$ is a leaf and no other receiver path uses $e$. The parameter-to-law map is then not injective.

Suppose a nonroot internal vertex $v$ is not split by any design. Let $e_0=(u,v)$ be its incoming edge and let $e_c=(v,c)$ range over its child edges. Since $p_{e_0}<1$ and each of the finitely many $p_{e_c}<1$, an open interval around $1$ keeps $tp_{e_0}<1$ and $p_{e_c}/t<1$ for every child; all changed probabilities remain positive there. Choose $t\ne1$ in that interval. Define $p'_{e_0}=tp_{e_0}$ and $p'_{e_c}=p_{e_c}/t$, leaving every other probability fixed. Then $p'_{e_0}p'_{e_c}=p_{e_0}p_{e_c}$ for every child $c$. In each design, receivers below $v$, if any, lie in one child subtree $c$; their outcomes all contain the common factor $B=X_{e_0}X_{e_c}$. This factor is Bernoulli with the same success probability under $p$ and $p'$, and is independent of every other link variable. Receivers outside that child subtree use no changed edge; their possible shared ancestor variables remain unchanged and independent of $B$. Thus the joint receiver-outcome law for every design is unchanged, although $p'\ne p$.

Let $v$ be a nonroot internal vertex. By [F2], some design contains receivers $r,s$ in distinct child subtrees of $v$; since $T$ is a tree their last common vertex on the root paths is $v$. Write $a_r=\prod_{e\in P(v,r)}p_e$ and $a_s=\prod_{e\in P(v,s)}p_e$. Independence in [F1] gives $m_r=q_va_r$, $m_s=q_va_s$, and $m_{rs}:=\Pr_p(Y_r=Y_s=1)=q_va_ra_s$. All factors are positive, so $m_{rs}>0$ and $q_v=m_rm_s/m_{rs}$. Hence the law determines $q_v$ for every nonroot internal vertex.

The value $q_o=1$ is fixed; steps 1.1 and 2.1 determine $q_v$ for every other vertex. For each edge $e=(u,v)$, $p_e=q_v/q_u$, with $q_u>0$. Therefore equal experiment laws give equal $p_e$ on every edge, so $\mathsf L$ is injective. By [F3], the link-probability identity target is identifiable.

If the split/coverage condition fails, either a receiver is uncovered or a nonroot internal vertex is not split. Steps 1.2 and 1.3 give two distinct parameter vectors with the same full sampling law in either case. Thus injectivity of $\mathsf L$ implies the condition; together with step 3.1 this proves the equivalence.

Only finite choices; no AC. Published F3 has a nonfatal reference-placement defect only. No mathematical edit or finite-smoke substitution.

derivations.claim: Under unicast to $r_i$, success has probability $p_0p_i$. Both parameter vectors give $p_0p_1=1/4$ and $p_0p_2=1/8$. Independence across probes makes each unicast outcome sequence have the same Bernoulli-product law under both vectors, and the separate schemes therefore have the same joint law.

Under multicast, the receiver marginals are $m_1=p_0p_1=1/4$ and $m_2=p_0p_2=1/8$, while the joint success probability is $m_{12}=p_0p_1p_2$. It is $1/16$ for the first vector and $3/32$ for the second, so their multicast laws differ.

For any interior vector, the multicast law supplies $m_1,m_2,m_{12}$, with $m_{12}>0$. The equations give $p_0=m_1m_2/m_{12}$, $p_1=m_1/p_0$, and $p_2=m_2/p_0$. Thus the multicast law determines every link probability.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

derivations.claim: On one probability space carrying independent $Z_0,Z_1,Z_2\sim N(0,1)$, set $X_i^{\mu}=\mu_i+Z_i$ and $X_i^{\mu'}=\mu_i'+Z_i$. By [F1], each vector has the required independent link-delay laws.

For $\mu=(0,0,0)$ the observation vector is $(Z_0+Z_1,Z_0+Z_2)$. For $\mu'=(1,-1,-1)$ it is $((1+Z_0)+(-1+Z_1),(1+Z_0)+(-1+Z_2))=(Z_0+Z_1,Z_0+Z_2)$. Thus the two observation vectors are equal on this coupling and have the same joint law; independent repetitions also have the same law.
The mean vectors are distinct, so [F2] implies that the identity link-mean target is not identifiable from the observed path-delay law.
